title: Classical Christian Dictionary #4
author: Wilson, Doug
summary: Doug Wilson's Classical Christian Dictionary continues its tour of Latin phrases essential to classical Christian education, covering terms from ad nauseam to soli Deo gloria. Each entry combines etymological precision with Wilson's characteristic wit—from carpe crustulum ('seize the cookie') to the gravitas of the five Reformation solas. The entries model how classical educators transmit both the forms and the spirit of the Latin tradition, while clarifying common confusions between e.g. and i.e., etc. and et al.
points: Common Latin abbreviations like e.g., i.e., ibid., and etc. have carefully distinct uses that classical educators and students must keep separated—confusion between e.g. and i.e. is especially widespread.
The five solas of the Reformation—sola fide, sola gratia, solus Christus, sola Scriptura, soli Deo gloria—provide a theological framework worth teaching as Latin phrases with doctrinal weight.
In loco parentis defines the derivative nature of teacher authority: teachers exercise authority over students on behalf of parents, at the pleasure of parents, not independently.
Sic ('thus he says') signals verbatim accuracy in quotation even when the quoted material contains errors—essential scholarly citation practice for classical students.
Latin phrases like deo volente and mea culpa connect daily speech to a worldview where God's will governs human plans and personal responsibility is taken seriously.
quotes: Sic—this means thus, and is short for “thus he says.” You would use this when you are quoting someone, and you want to reproduce the quote exactly, but whoever it was made a mistake in that quote, and you don’t want people to think it was you.

It means “my fault.” If they were really bad, you might have them say mea maxima culpa—“my most grievous fault.” Mutatis mutandis—if you are going from one situation to another, and they are not exactly alike, you would say this.

Ibid.—this is an abbreviation, hence the period, and is short for ibidem, which means “in the same place.” It is used in footnotes to indicate that you are citing the same book you just cited previously.

Soli Deo gloria—this is one of the five watchwords of the Reformation, and means “glory to God alone.” Solus Christus—this means “Christ alone,” and is another of the five watchwords of the Reformation.
It means “without which not.” Sola fide—this means “faith alone.” It refers to the Protestant doctrine that teaches that faith is the only instrument to receive the grace of God in Christ.
It means “with a grain of salt.” Cum laude—this phrase will most likely show up in your graduation ceremonies, and it means “with praise.” It is the bronze medal of Latin kudos.
